title: The shortest way to Tokyo
hook: On a flat map the straight line looks shortest. Fly it on a globe and see.

knows: what a flat world map looks like
that a flight from New York to Tokyo crosses the Pacific
doesNotKnow: why the shortest path looks bent on most flat maps

misconception: The shortest route is the straight line you draw on the map.
objective: The learner can explain that the shortest path on a sphere is a great circle, which bows toward the pole and looks bent on a Mercator map, while the map's straight line is longer.

claims.text: The shortest path over the globe from New York (JFK) to Tokyo (Haneda) is about 10,880 km.
claims.source: Great-circle distance on a sphere of radius 6,371.0088 km (kit EARTH_RADIUS_KM) with d3-geo geoDistance: 10,875.5 km, shown rounded to 10 km. Coordinates JFK 40.640 N 73.779 W, HND 35.549 N 139.780 E (OurAirports / airport authority; coordinates not independently checked). Script: artifacts/scratch/w1-tokyo.mjs.

claims.text: That shortest path bows north to about 70°N, passing over northern Alaska.
claims.source: Sampling geoInterpolate(JFK, HND): northernmost point 69.85 N, 145.41 W; geoContains on the kit's 1:110m 'United States of America' shape is true there. 1:110m coastline is coarse; the point is inland of the Beaufort Sea coast by a small margin in this data.

claims.text: The straight line on this Mercator map, a line of constant compass bearing, is about 12,820 km, about 18% longer than the shortest path.
claims.source: Rhumb-line length formula (Snyder 1987, Map Projections: A Working Manual, USGS PP 1395, ch. 7 on Mercator loxodromes): 12,818.1 km the short way west; ratio 1.1786. A straight line on Mercator is a rhumb line because Mercator is conformal (same source).

claims.text: Great-circle routes via Honolulu and via Mexico City are about 14,200 km and 14,680 km.
claims.source: Sum of two geoDistance legs, R = 6,371.0088 km: via Honolulu (21.307 N, 157.858 W) 14,201 km; via Mexico City (19.433 N, 99.133 W) 14,678 km. Gazetteer coordinates not independently checked.

claims.text: On a sphere the shortest path between two points is an arc of a great circle.
claims.source: Standard spherical geometry; Snyder (1987) ch. 5; any text on geodesics on the sphere.

claims.text: Mercator stretches the map more the farther it is from the equator.
claims.source: Snyder (1987) ch. 7: Mercator scale factor k = sec(latitude).

claims.text: Real flights also bend for winds and airspace; this lesson ignores them.
claims.source: Modelling choice stated to the learner. The lesson makes no claim about any airline's actual path.

recall.question: Two cities are both far north of the equator, on opposite sides of an ocean. On a Mercator map, the shortest flight between them usually looks:
recall.why: The shortest path on a sphere is a great circle, which bends toward the pole between two northern cities; Mercator draws it as a curve.
